note: Every proportion here names where it came from, because a builder that invented recipes would undo the rest of this site. Where a free-to-use recipe exists it is used in its own ratios and credited. Where none exists — and for a cayenne-and-butter wing sauce none does — the proportions are this project's own and say so under the result. Sugar under each result is computed from the quantities on screen, at 12.6 g of sugar in a tablespoon of sugar, 17 g in honey, 10 g in molasses and 3.7 g in ketchup, and drawn against the bottles read for the sauce page. A sauce you make generally lands nowhere near them.

bases.name: Cayenne and butter
bases.region: Buffalo, and every bar that copied it
bases.says: Two ingredients doing the work. Butter carries the pepper and nothing thickens it.

anchor.note: No free-to-use Buffalo wing sauce recipe exists to build on: the Anchor Bar's is a trade secret and the bottle recipes are somebody's copyright. Cited here is only what the sauce IS — a vinegar-based cayenne pepper sauce cut with melted butter, sometimes with Worcestershire and garlic powder. The ratio here is this project's own, and a cook who wants it milder pours more butter, which is exactly how a bar does it.

ingredients.name: cayenne pepper sauce
ingredients.unit_hint: Frank's RedHot or Crystal — the thin, vinegary kind, not a thick chilli sauce

method: Melt the butter gently. Do not brown it.
Whisk the pepper sauce in off the heat, then the vinegar, the Worcestershire and the garlic.
Hold it warm. It splits if it sits; whisk it back together.
Fry the wings first, sauce them after, in a metal bowl, shaken.

bases.name: Lemon pepper, wet
bases.says: Dry seasoning loosened in butter until it clings. Order it dry and you skip the second step.

anchor.title: Cookbook:Lemon Pepper
anchor.note: Wikibooks names what goes in a lemon-pepper blend — dehydrated lemon zest and black pepper, often with salt, garlic and onion powders and citric acid — and gives no amounts at all. The components are its; the proportions below are ours.

method: Melt the butter and take it off the heat.
Stir the seasoning, the zest and the garlic through it.
Add the lemon juice last so it stays bright.
Toss the wings in it, then dust with more dry seasoning at the end.

bases.name: Jerk
bases.region: Jamaica, by way of Brooklyn, the Bronx, Miami and Hartford
bases.says: Allspice, thyme and chile. A marinade before the fire, not a sauce after it.

anchor.title: Cookbook:Jamaican Jerk Spice I
anchor.note: The dry spice below keeps the Wikibooks recipe's own ratios — cayenne, cinnamon, nutmeg, allspice, onion powder, thyme, sugar, dried onion, salt. The oil, lime and soy that turn it into a wet marinade are ours.

method: Combine the dry spices first and keep what you do not use in a sealed jar.
Whisk the oil, lime and soy into the spice until it is a loose paste.
Coat the wings and leave them cold for at least four hours, overnight if you can.
Grill or roast them. Jerk wants live fire or a hot oven, not a fryer.

bases.name: Soy and sweet
bases.region: Japanese and Korean American kitchens, and every wing menu since the 1990s
bases.says: Soy, mirin, sugar. It glazes rather than coats, and it burns if the pan is hot.

anchor.title: Cookbook:Teriyaki Sauce
anchor.note: Scaled from the recipe's own two-parts-soy, two-parts-mirin, one-part-brown-sugar, with its teaspoon each of ginger and garlic. The proportions are the recipe's. Teriyaki is Japanese; the Korean American wing it sits beside on a menu is a different sauce with a different history, and that record says so.

method: Warm everything in a small pan over a low heat until the sugar dissolves.
Do not boil it down unless you want a glaze; it thickens as it cools.
Brush it on fried wings rather than tossing them, or it slides off.
A half teaspoon of cornstarch boiled in will hold it on, per the recipe's own note.

bases.name: Hot honey
bases.says: Sweet first, then the burn arrives late. The most recent thing on this list by decades.

anchor.note: No free-to-use recipe carries this one. The proportions are ours, built to keep honey first on the list, which is where every commercial bottle puts it.

method: Warm the honey with the flakes until it loosens. Do not let it catch.
Off the heat, stir in the vinegar, the pepper sauce and the salt.
Leave it an hour so the flakes give up their heat, then strain if you want it clear.
Drizzle rather than toss; it sets on a cooling wing.

bases.name: Alabama white
bases.region: north Alabama, and the smokers that borrowed it
bases.says: Mayonnaise, vinegar and black pepper. Thin, sharp, and it breaks over heat.

anchor.note: Composed from the sauce record's cited description — mayonnaise, vinegar, black pepper, lemon, sometimes horseradish. Big Bob Gibson's own formula is not published, and nothing here claims to be it.

method: Whisk everything cold. It wants to be pourable, not spoonable.
Rest it overnight if you can; the pepper needs the time.
Dunk smoked wings in it straight off the cooker, or serve it in a cup.
Keep it off direct heat. Mayonnaise splits.

bases.name: Garlic and parmesan
bases.region: the pizzeria, and then the whole country
bases.says: Butter, garlic, cheese. The one flavour on a wing menu that owes nothing to a pepper.

anchor.note: No free-to-use recipe exists for the wing version. Composed to keep butter first and cheese fine enough to cling, which is what the sauce record describes.

method: Warm the butter and oil with the garlic until the garlic smells sweet, not brown.
Take it off the heat before the cheese goes in, or the cheese turns to string.
Toss the wings, then finish with more cheese and the parsley.
Grate the cheese finer than feels necessary. Coarse cheese falls off.
